item.title: Hamburg tribunal confirms it will deliver its Sea Lion order on November 28
item.description: The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea has confirmed it will announce on Saturday, November 28, at noon Hamburg time — 8 a.m. in Montevideo and Buenos Aires — its decision on Argentina’s request for provisional measures to halt the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands. The order will be read at a public sitting by the tribunal’s president, Judge Maurice Kamga.

item.title: Argentina’s lower house debates Falklands sovereignty bill today, with one chapter short of votes
item.description: Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies debates the national sovereignty defence bill from noon on Wednesday, legislation that toughens sanctions for unauthorised resource exploitation in the Falklands. Javier Milei’s government is confident of passing it in general, but does not have the votes secured for the chapter on foreign interference, which requires a special majority.

item.title: Argentina calls Princess Anne’s visit to the Falklands a “provocation”
item.description: The Argentine government on Tuesday rejected the visit by Princess Anne, the sister of King Charles III, to the Falklands and South Georgia, calling it a “provocation” at a time when the United Kingdom, according to Buenos Aires, is advancing hydrocarbon exploitation in waters whose sovereignty Argentina claims. The Princess has been in the archipelago since November 9.

item.title: Haitians rally behind Bukele as Salvadoran troops battle gangs
item.description: Thousands of Haitians took to the streets on Tuesday to urge El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele to keep fighting gangs, as his troops bolster security forces in the Caribbean nation. But experts warn that growing public support could turn to anger without a long-term plan to tackle violence and strengthen Haiti's police.

item.title: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life
item.description:
Indigenous Awá people of Amazon make contact with villagers and accept food to take back to territory

About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.

According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.

item.title: US, Mexico and Bolivia lose measles-free status as deaths mount
item.description: The US has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus has spread at the fastest rate in more than 30 years, while Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles-elimination status. Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases, in the US and globally, and measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024.

item.title: Costa Rican journalist shot dead in first such killing in 25 years
item.description:
Camilo Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence

The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against ⁠suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot dead on Monday, authorities said.

The first known killing of a journalist ⁠in Costa Rica in ⁠25 years, ​Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence driven by international trafficking groups, despite long ⁠being regarded as one of Central America’s most peaceful and stable democracies.

item.title: Bows and old guns: Indigenous militias left to fight Peru’s cocaine gangs alone
item.description:
Decades after Lima armed them to fight Shining Path rebels, the Asháninka are still defending their Amazon rainforest, but now against drug traffickers – and without any help

Shielding his eyes from the tropical sun, Irmeo Sánchez Gómez – better known by his nom de guerre, Kiri – pointed up at a weathered shed on top of a hill, a few frayed sandbags piled at its base. Beyond it, the Tambo River snaked through Peru’s Amazonian rainforest.

“When the terrorists came,” Kiri says, “they would shoot up at us from the riverbank. Without guns of our own, we defended ourselves with bows and arrows. Later, the army gave us guns and built these defences.”

item.title: Guatemala Profile
item.description:
Guatemala Profile

Guatemala's criminal organizations are among the most sophisticated and dangerous in Central America. Some of them have been in operation for decades. They include former members of the military, intelligence agencies and active members of the police. Transporting illegal drugs north comprises the bulk of their activity, but organized crime in Guatemala is also involved in marijuana and poppy cultivation, as well as human trafficking, kidnapping, extortion, money laundering, arms smuggling, adoption rings, eco trafficking and other illegal enterprises. They often work with groups from Mexico, Colombia and other Central American nations and they have the potential to expand and command other Central American nations' underworlds. Read more

The post Guatemala Profile appeared first on InSight Crime.

item.title: November 17 blackout hoax: How a conspiracy theory went viral around the world
item.description: A conspiracy theory claiming a worldwide "blackout" will hit the world on November 17 has spread across social media, with the claim it will cut electricity, internet and banking services. The rumour stems from a routine US FEMA emergency alert test, but was amplified by cryptocurrency accounts, misleading claims about EU preparedness advice and references to "The Simpsons". Recent technology outages, flight disruptions and cyberattacks have added to public anxiety, helping turn a routine test into a global hoax.
